procedural_history.originating_court: Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate 5th Court Dadar
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 23rd/24th August, 1973 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal Nos. 68, 298 & 510 of 1972.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused preferred three appeals in the High Court of Bombay against the order of conviction and sentence passed against them by the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate. These appeals were heard by a single Judge of the High Court and by a common Judgment dated 27th August 1973 the learned single Judge confirmed the conviction of the accused under Section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and Section 5 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act 1947 but set aside the conviction under Section 135 (I) (a) (ii) of the Customs Act 1962 and Section 23 ·(t A) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1973.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Assistant Collector of Customs accepted the judgment of the learned single Judge in so far as it acquitted the accused of the offence under Section 23 (I A) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1973 but he was aggrieved by that part of the judgment which set aside the conviction under Section 135 (1) (a) (ii) of the Customs Act 1962 and he accordingly preferred the present three appeals with special leave obtained from this Court.

decision.conviction_status: The order of the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate convicting the accused is restored.
decision.sentence_status: The order of the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate sentencing the accused is restored.
directions: The Order of acquittal passed by the learned single Judge of the High Court is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the conviction of the accused under section 135(1)(a)(ii) of the Customs Act, 1962.

facts: Customs officials apprehended the accused on a fishing vessel off the coast of Bombay.
The officials found 194 ingots of silver in the vessel, which they believed were being smuggled out of India.
The accused were prosecuted and convicted by the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate for several offences, including under Section 135(1)(a)(ii) of the Customs Act.
On appeal, the High Court set aside the conviction under the Customs Act, leading to this appeal by the Assistant Collector of Customs to the Supreme Court.
law: The central legal provision was Section 135(1)(a)(ii) of the Customs Act, 1962.
This section penalizes anyone who is knowingly concerned in any fraudulent evasion or attempt at evasion of:
1. Any duty chargeable on goods, OR
2. Any prohibition imposed on such goods under the Customs Act or any other law.
application: The High Court had acquitted the accused based on their argument that the words "with respect to such goods" at the end of the section referred only to goods on which duty was chargeable (the first part of the section). Since no duty was chargeable on the export of silver, the High Court concluded the section did not apply.
The Supreme Court rejected this interpretation as "plainly erroneous."

The Court explained that the section has three distinct parts: the first deals with evading duty, while the second and third parts deal with evading a *prohibition* on goods, regardless of whether duty is chargeable.
It clarified that the phrase "such goods" refers back to the term "any goods" at the beginning of the section, not just to dutiable goods.

The accused were attempting to evade the prohibition on the export of silver, which was imposed under the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947. This action fell squarely under the third part of Section 135(1)(a)(ii), which covers the evasion of a prohibition imposed by "any other law."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was incorrect in its interpretation of the law. It held that the accused's attempt to smuggle silver was a clear violation of the prohibition on its export, making them guilty under Section 135(1)(a)(ii) of the Customs Act. Therefore, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's acquittal, and restored the original conviction and sentence from the trial court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the conviction of the accused under section 135(1)(a)(ii) of the Customs Act, 1962.
appellant_arguments: The accused were knowingly concerned with the fraudulent evasion or attempt at evasion of the prohibition on the export of silver without a licence, which was imposed under the Export Trade Control Order of 1968.
This act of attempting to evade the prohibition on exporting silver plainly falls under the offense described in section 135(1)(a)(ii) of the Customs Act.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's arguments are not specified in the provided text.

cases.principle: To point out that the High Court's view in the present case—that goods must be chargeable with duty to fall under the latter parts of section 135(1)(a)(ii)—had already been overruled by a Division Bench of the same High Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where goods are chargeable to duty and a person is knowingly concerned in the fraudulent evasion or attempted evasion of that duty, the case falls under the first part of section 135(1)(a)(ii) of the Customs Act, 1962. However, where a prohibition is imposed on any goods under the Customs Act or any other law, then irrespective of whether duty is chargeable, any person knowingly concerned in the fraudulent evasion or attempted evasion of such prohibition is punishable under the third part of that section.
obiter: The view taken by the learned single judge of the High Court has been subsequently overruled by a Division Bench of the same High Court.
Section 135(1)(a)(ii) is structurally divisible into three parts.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court determined that section 135(1)(a) of the Customs Act, 1962, contains distinct parts. The first part deals with the fraudulent evasion of duty on goods that are chargeable with duty. The second and third parts, however, pertain to the fraudulent evasion of any prohibition imposed on any goods under the Customs Act or any other law, irrespective of whether duty is chargeable on such goods. The court clarified that the concluding phrase "with respect to such goods" refers back to "any goods" mentioned at the commencement of the section, not exclusively to the "goods chargeable with duty" from the first part. As the accused were knowingly involved in an attempt to evade the prohibition on exporting silver without a license (a prohibition imposed by the Export Trade Control Order 1968), their case was plainly covered by the third part of the section.
legal_tests_applied: Plain natural construction of the language used in a statute.
